title: Southern Ocean
wiki_lead:
The Southern Ocean, also known as the Antarctic Ocean, comprises the southernmost waters of the World Ocean, generally taken to be south of 60° S latitude and encircling Antarctica. With a size of 21,960,000 km2 (8,480,000 mi2), it is the second-smallest of the five principal oceanic divisions, smaller than the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian oceans, and larger than the Arctic Ocean.
The maximum depth of the Southern Ocean, using the definition that it lies south of 60th parallel, was surveyed by the Five Deeps Expedition in early February 2019. The expedition's multibeam sonar team identified the deepest point at 60° 28' 46"S, 025° 32' 32"W, with a depth of 7,434 metres (24,390 ft). The expedition leader and chief submersible pilot, Victor Vescovo, has proposed naming this deepest point the "Factorian Deep", based on the name of the crewed submersible DSV Limiting Factor, in which he successfully visited the bottom for the first time on 3 February 2019.
By way of his voyages in the 1770s, James Cook proved that waters encompassed the southern latitudes of the globe. Yet, geographers have often disagreed on whether the Southern Ocean should be defined as a body of water bound by the seasonally fluctuating Antarctic Convergence — an oceanic zone where cold, northward flowing waters from the Antarctic mix with warmer Subantarctic waters — or not defined at all, with its waters instead treated as the southern limits of the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian oceans. In 2000, the International Hydrographic Organization (IHO) finally settled the debate after the full importance of Southern Ocean overturning circulation had been ascertained, and the term Southern Ocean now defines the body of water which lies south of the northern limit of that circulation.
The Southern Ocean overturning circulation is important because it makes up the second half of the global thermohaline circulation, after the better known Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC). Much like AMOC, it has also been substantially affected by climate change, in ways that have increased ocean stratification, and which may also result in the circulation substantially slowing or even passing a tipping point and collapsing outright. The latter would have adverse impacts on global weather and the function of marine ecosystems here, unfolding over centuries. The ongoing warming is already changing marine ecosystems here.

Definition and term use

Borders and names for oceans and seas were internationally agreed when the International Hydrographic Bureau, the precursor to the IHO, convened the First International Conference on 24 July 1919. The IHO then published these in its Limits of Oceans and Seas, the first edition being 1928. Since the first edition, the limits of the Southern Ocean have moved progressively southward; since 1953, it has been omitted from the official publication and left to local hydrographic offices to determine their own limits.
The IHO included the ocean and its definition as the waters south of the 60th parallel south in its 2000 revisions, but this has not been formally adopted, due to continuing impasses about some of the content, such as the naming dispute over the Sea of Japan. The 2000 IHO definition was circulated as a draft edition in 2002, and is used by some within the IHO and other organizations, such as the CIA World Factbook and Merriam-Webster.
The Australian Government regards the Southern Ocean as lying immediately south of Australia (see § Australian standpoint).
The National Geographic Society recognized the ocean officially in June 2021. Prior to this, it depicted it in a typeface different from the other world oceans; instead, it showed the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian Oceans extending to Antarctica on both its print and online maps. Map publishers using the term Southern Ocean on their maps include Hema Maps and GeoNova.

grok_lead: The Southern Ocean is the circumpolar body of water encircling Antarctica, extending from the continental coast northward to 60Â° south latitude, where its northern boundary coincides with the Antarctic Circumpolar Current (ACC) that functionally separates it from the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans. This definition, increasingly adopted by international bodies, emphasizes oceanographic criteria over arbitrary latitudinal lines, reflecting the ACC's role as the world's strongest current, transporting approximately 130-150 million cubic meters of water per second eastward and isolating Antarctica's cold waters from warmer northern flows. Covering about 20.3 million square kilometers with a volume of roughly 71 million cubic kilometers, it constitutes the second-smallest principal ocean division but exerts disproportionate influence on global thermohaline circulation, carbon sequestration, and nutrient upwelling. Defined by relentless westerly winds and the ACC's unbroken flowâthe only such circumpolar current due to the absence of continental barriersâthe Southern Ocean features extreme conditions, including the planet's strongest winds, largest waves, and city-sized icebergs calved from Antarctic ice shelves. Its waters drive deep convection and intermediate water formation, ventilating the global ocean and regulating Earth's climate by absorbing heat and CO2 at rates exceeding other oceans, though this capacity is modulated by wind-driven upwelling and sea ice dynamics. Biologically, it supports vast krill swarms foundational to Antarctic food webs, sustaining penguins, seals, whales, and fisheries, while its remoteness and harsh environment limit human activity primarily to scientific research stations governed under the Antarctic Treaty System. Recognition as a distinct ocean remains contested, with traditional hydrographic classifications subsuming its waters into southern extensions of the three major ocean s, but formal acknowledgment by entities like the U.S. Board on Geographic Names since 1999, NOAA in 2021, and a 2023 IHO proposal for 60Â°S limits underscore its unique geophysical identity amid evolving oceanographic understanding. This delineation highlights causal distinctions in circulation and ecology rather than political or arbitrary boundaries, countering earlier maps that variably depicted southern seas without unified nomenclature.
